content.text: Where we dive deeper into React and construct a realtime collaborative post-it note app with React!

We will start with a version of the app that does not have a backend, it’ll use state for notes but if you refresh the page all your hard work will disappear — and it’ll only work in one browser window.

Then we will add in Firebase for persistent storage. Firebase is a backend as a service (BAAS). It provides a simple JSON data store (

A post-it note style app where users can add notes, move them around, edit them, and delete them. This React app will use Firebase as its backend to store collections of notes. The position of notes will also be stored, so people in multiple browsers can edit and arrange them in real-time. The notes themselves will support markdown notation and editing.
For Part 1, the app will store state in memory only and won’t use Firebase yet. But here are the overall specs of the full project.

We’ve discussed how mutable data structures can be dangerous and unpleasant — data changing without you knowing about, etc. React is built around the idea that state in particular should be immutable. You have
states, but you don’t alter existing state. As we dig deeper into react and functional programming we’ll see the insistence on
functions and immutable data more and more.
For this assignment we’re going to play with a library for making our state immutable and easier to work with at the same time.

in Part 2 we’ll be handing over state to Firebase and we are going to structure our data to make that easier / more similar to how firebase works.

🐙 Before we continue let’s make sure we’ve committed and pushed everything.

Now that we have a working stand-alone app, we should connect it to backend to make it cool and collaborative, MULTI-USER and COLLABORATIVE! We need persistent storage to enable our notes to not go away on reload and to synchronize the notes across different instances of the app.
One way to add persistent storage is to use a backend as a service (BAAS) platform. Firebase is one such platform that provides a JSON based database (
) that has some nice realtime properties. For instance you can subscribe to change events on collections of objects. Can we use Firebase with our React app? You bet!
Note: we'll be using Firebase Realtime Database for this rather than the newer Cloud Firestore, although both would work for our purposes.
This lab documents Firebase, but you are
to explore other platforms! Each has different strengths:
— Open-source, PostgreSQL-based (full SQL support), self-hostable, great if you prefer relational data
— TypeScript-first with automatic realtime subscriptions and ACID transactions
— Collaboration infrastructure with built-in presence, comments, and CRDT support
— Edge-first realtime with WebSocket rooms, great for multiplayer experiences
All of these support realtime updates and would work for this assignment. If you choose an alternative, document your experience — we'd love to hear what worked!

Firebase stores everything as JSON — in fact the whole thing can be thought of as a JSON tree. This works pretty well with how we’ve already been thinking of our notes app data-structures. Everything we needed we stored in a Map, which essentially is a javascript object called notes, with individual notes underneath it stored by key. We created our own key but now Firebase will just handle all the data storage for us. All we need to do is figure out how.
Here’s what our data might look like in firebase:
Firebase’s realtime database is based on subscribing to events! This should sound familiar.

In our case, since we are storing the full state of our notes in a top level notes state object, we should subscribe to the on value change Firebase event on all of notes. This isn’t always the best, in most cases you actually want to subscribe to things lower down in the tree. For our app with a single board of notes though, we might as well subscribe to all the displayed notes.

Advanced Extra Credit: CRDTs for Conflict-Free Collaboration
This is a challenging extra credit that explores technology used by apps like Figma and Linear.

Our Firebase implementation works, but what happens when two users edit the same note simultaneously? Firebase uses "last write wins" — one user's changes get overwritten. For real collaborative editing, this is a problem.
(Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) solve this. They're data structures where concurrent edits from multiple users
— no conflicts, no data loss. The CRDT handles merging locally, and you use Firebase to sync changes between clients.
Firebase stores and maybe broadcasts CRDT updates or use a public service for this
The CRDT library handles conflict resolution automatically
Add a CRDT layer to your notes app. You have options:

to manage state locally, and sync updates through Firebase. Loro is particularly interesting — it has built-in version control (checkout any historical state, like git for your data) and a native moveable tree CRDT (perfect for reordering notes).
Use a backend service that provides CRDT sync out of the box (e.g.,
, or others). These handle the sync infrastructure for you. Not as impressive but still fun.
Demonstrate conflict-free merging when two users edit simultaneously
